title: Curtius rearrangement
subtitle: An acyl azide loses N₂ on heating; the isocyanate is trapped by tert-butanol

reactants.caption: benzoyl azide (drawn as N⁻–N⁺≡N) in tert-butanol
reactants.learnerPrompt: Heat: nitrogen gas leaves and a group moves to nitrogen.
hintTiers: The azide can lose N₂, a very stable molecule. Which group on the carbonyl carbon can move to the nitrogen that N₂ leaves behind?
Three arrows: the N–N bond breaks onto the N₂ nitrogen, the phenyl–carbonyl bond moves to the nitrogen next to the carbonyl, and a lone pair on that nitrogen makes C=N.

N–N bond (the one to the carbonyl side) → a lone pair on the N₂ nitrogen; bond from the carbonyl carbon to the ring → new bond from the ring carbon to the nitrogen next to the carbonyl; that nitrogen's lone pair → C=N π bond.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: tert-Butanol is a weak, crowded nucleophile, and the acyl azide rearranges first on heating. The alcohol reacts later, with the isocyanate.
Oxygen keeps its C=O. The phenyl group moves to nitrogen, the atom that loses N₂.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right that N₂ leaves, but alone that gives an acyl nitrene, with nitrogen short of an octet. Under heating the phenyl group moves as N₂ goes, and a nitrogen lone pair makes C=N.

isocyanate.caption: phenyl isocyanate + N₂ + tert-butanol
hintTiers: The central carbon of N=C=O is between two electronegative atoms: very electrophilic. Which nucleophile is present?
The alcohol oxygen bonds to the central carbon, and the C=N π pair moves onto nitrogen. Two arrows.
Alcohol oxygen lone pair → new bond to the isocyanate carbon; C=N π bond → a lone pair on nitrogen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Nitrogen is not the electrophilic atom. The carbon between nitrogen and oxygen is.
N₂ is unreactive: it just bubbles away. The alcohol adds to the isocyanate.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the oxygen bonds to the central carbon. Now carbon has five bonds: move the C=N π pair onto nitrogen.

zwitterion.caption: the adduct: positive oxygen, negative nitrogen
hintTiers: A positive oxygen with an O–H sits next to a negative nitrogen. What makes the adduct neutral?
The nitrogen lone pair takes the proton from the positive oxygen; the O–H pair stays on oxygen. Two arrows.
Nitrogen lone pair → new bond to the drawn O–H hydrogen; that O–H bond → a lone pair on oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing the alcohol goes back to the isocyanate. Move the proton instead.

steps.explanationAfterStep: N₂ leaves as the phenyl group moves from carbon to nitrogen with its bonding pair: one concerted step, with no free nitrene. Loss of the very stable N₂ drives it. The migrating group keeps its configuration.
The alcohol adds to the central carbon of the isocyanate.
Also correct: the proton can move to nitrogen as the oxygen adds, in one step.

The proton moves from oxygen to nitrogen (in practice relayed by another alcohol molecule): a carbamate. Acid removes the tert-butyl group to give aniline (see Protecting groups). With water instead of an alcohol, the isocyanate gives a carbamic acid, which loses CO₂ to give the amine directly.

mechanismSummary: On heating, benzoyl azide loses N₂ as the phenyl group moves from the carbonyl carbon to nitrogen, in one concerted step: phenyl isocyanate. tert-Butanol, the solvent, adds to the central carbon of the isocyanate, and a proton transfer gives the carbamate. The Curtius, Hofmann and Lossen rearrangements all make an isocyanate in the same way: a group moves to an electron-poor nitrogen as a leaving group goes.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 38
